Next month the 26th marks the one-year anniversary of the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po. The independent committee investigating the fire is expected to submit its report to the Chief Executive before the end of October. Recent reports indicated that the government has activated the accountability system for department heads to investigate administrative responsibility for the fire, and has redeployed policy secretaries to assist. Chief Executive John Lee today (the 6th) did not respond to whether the mechanism had been activated, stating that the government had made a series of arrangements and would push forward reforms and hold those responsible accountable as soon as possible after the report is submitted. The luxury residence One Stanley in Stanley was exposed for having steel reinforcement not matching the approved plans. Lee stated that the Buildings Department is investigating the case, and that he has asked the Development Bureau to oversee the investigation. As several construction projects have been exposed for problems one after another, he said he attaches great importance to the construction quality of building projects in Hong Kong, which concerns the professional standards, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction industry, and that the government will strictly enforce the law.

Nearly one year after the Wang Fuk Court fire, the independent committee is expected to submit its report before the end of October. (File photo)

Earlier media reports stated that two policy secretaries—former Deputy Secretary for Security Eric Mok and Commissioner for Sports Choi Kin-bun—would provide support to an investigation sub-group under the Public Service Commission, dedicated to preliminary work on administrative accountability.

Chief Executive John Lee met the media before attending the Executive Council meeting this morning. When asked whether the reports were accurate, and whether the activation of the accountability system for department heads to investigate responsibility meant that even if there were reports, accountability involving officials would not yield results immediately, and how long the public would have to wait,

Lee stated that he had made it clear from the start that after the independent committee submitted its report, he would actively study and follow up on its recommendations, implement reforms and announce details. He did not directly respond to whether policy secretaries had already been redeployed to prepare for preliminary investigative work, only saying that "the government has made a series of arrangements during this period," emphasising that once submitted, based on the contents of the report, "comprehensive reforms would be pushed forward as soon as possible in the short term, and accountability pursued," with detailed announcements to follow.

Lee stated that after the independent committee submits its report, reforms and accountability would be pursued as soon as possible based on its contents. (File photo)

Lee also reiterated multiple times that improvement measures cannot wait. Therefore, when delivering the Policy Address in September, he announced seven priority improvement measures, including banning smoking at construction sites, strengthening regulation of fire service installations, enhancing disciplinary action and punishment for professionals and contractors, improving compliance in owners' corporations, studying the criminalisation of bid-rigging, providing for the first time tendering and bid evaluation services, formulating pre-qualification lists for consultants and contractors, and studying solutions to better assist the public on matters relating to the professional nature of projects.

According to records, the Public Service Commission is an independent statutory advisory body that advises the Chief Executive on civil service appointments, promotions and disciplinary matters. The accountability system for department heads was proposed by Chief Executive John Lee in last year's Policy Address, establishing a two-tier investigation mechanism based on the severity of departmental issues. For less serious or isolated incidents, department heads will conduct the first-tier investigation. If a department has serious problems, or involves extensive, repetitive systemic issues, or may involve the role of the department head, an investigation sub-group led by the Public Service Commission will conduct the second-tier investigation.

The luxury residence One Stanley was exposed for having units with steel reinforcement not matching the approved plans. Lee stated he would not comment on cases still under investigation, and has asked the Development Bureau to oversee the Buildings Department's investigation.

One Stanley "shoddy reinforcement" — Development Bureau required to oversee investigation

Recently, construction projects have been exposed for problems one after another, including tilted lift shafts in the new building of Queen Mary Hospital, concrete samples at a Tung Chung public housing estate failing to meet strength standards, and steel reinforcement in floor slabs at luxury residence One Stanley in Stanley not matching the approved plans. Lee was asked whether problems existed in construction and project supervision.

Responding to the issues with the One Stanley project, he stated that the Buildings Department is rigorously investigating the case, "ascertaining issues regarding construction quality and supervision, and will handle it strictly in accordance with the law." As the investigation is ongoing, he would not comment on the case details, and has asked the Development Bureau to monitor the investigation. However, he emphasised that he attaches great importance to construction quality in Hong Kong's building projects, "concerned about whether professionals related to the project have diligently supervised, and whether contractors have violated regulations during construction," adding that this concerns the professional standards, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction industry, and that the government will inevitably enforce the law strictly.

He has also asked the Development Bureau to enhance regulatory requirements and penalties in legal aspects for construction projects overall, to ensure the deterrent effect of legislation, severely punish those responsible for violations, and safeguard the professional standards, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction industry. The Development Bureau will submit proposed amendments to the Buildings Ordinance this year to strengthen regulation and enhance the disciplinary and penalty systems, and the authorities will advance this work at full speed.

Recent concerns about difficulties faced by nursing graduates in finding jobs have drawn attention. Lee stated that demand for nurses has long existed, and noted that the Hospital Authority currently has over 3,000 nursing vacancies that graduates may apply for. (File photo)

Executive Council member Tommy Cheung criticises "unions posing as people" — Lee states demand exists long-term

Discussion about nurses' difficulties in finding jobs has intensified recently. The origin was a phone-in segment on a radio programme after the Policy Address, in which a Mr. Kwok, who claimed to be a psychiatric nurse in a disciplined service, said his application for extended retirement was not approved, and that his daughter, who was studying nursing, was unemployed immediately after graduation. He challenged the Hospital Authority's introduction of mainland medical and nursing staff. Executive Council member Tommy Cheung subsequently questioned whether it was the unions "possibly posing as people making phone calls," and stated he would wholeheartedly support importing foreign talent.

When asked by reporters about the difficulties nursing graduates face in finding jobs, how to address the concentration of vacancies among senior nurses, and how to respond to the Executive Council member's remarks which were accused of aggravating social tensions, Lee stated that in every industry, there are cases of graduates not seeking employment immediately after graduation for individual reasons, or recruiting organisations selecting those who best fit their needs, "resulting in situations where some individuals are not hired." He emphasised that demand for nurses in society has always existed, especially as Hong Kong's healthcare sector continues to develop and the trend of an ageing population continues, "so recruitment figures will ultimately inevitably reflect this existing demand." Without specifying anyone, he also noted that "various discussions in society on this aspect can help everyone clarify the issues further."

Lee also pointed out that according to 2025/26 figures, of approximately 4,000 potential nursing graduates, about 2,500 actually applied to the Hospital Authority, meaning 1,500 applied for positions outside the Hospital Authority, while the Hospital Authority currently still has over 3,000 nursing vacancies. "Nursing graduates may apply, and have the chance of being hired."

Secretary for Health, Professor Lo Chung-mau, earlier accepted interviews with multiple media organisations, clarifying that the government's recruitment policy definitely prioritises local talent. Lee also reiterated that based on the Hospital Authority's current nursing workforce, "99.8% are Hong Kong locally trained nurses," clearly putting into practice the policy of prioritising local talent for hiring. He also noted that currently 40% of nurses work in the public healthcare system, while the remaining 60% work in other healthcare roles, such as community nursing, elderly care, rehabilitation services, and private medical institutions. He emphasised that demand for nurses in society exists in the long term. The government will, in accordance with healthcare service needs, exchange views with the industry and academia, and plan well for medical and nursing training and manpower development.
